dimension: Online learning for cold-start identification of the best performers: bandits, best-arm identification, successive/sequential halving, Hyperband/ASHA, racing algorithms, sample-complexity lower bounds, non-stationary detection, and contextual bandits
summary:
The founder's recursive-partition proposal is Sequential Halving with the wrong variable varied, wrapped around Computerized Adaptive Testing. Both exist, both are proven, and one published system is already his idea built and measured.

Sequential Halving (Karnin, Koren and Somekh, ICML 2013, Algorithm 2) gives every surviving arm an equal share of budget, keeps the better half, and repeats for ceil(log2 n) rounds. Error is at most 3 log2(n) exp(-T / (8 H2 log2 n)) with H2 = max_i i/Delta_i^2. The founder's loop is the same elimination skeleton; the difference is that halving varies BUDGET across rounds and holds the instrument fixed, whereas he varies DIFFICULTY and holds the budget at 1. Varying difficulty without an equating model makes round-1 and round-2 scores incommensurable, so no single total order exists over the roster. Item Response Theory is the equating machinery, and adaptive testing has used it since Lord's flexilevel test (1971) and Weiss's stradaptive model (1973).

The sample-complexity bounds are decisive on his "2 or 3 attempts" claim. Mannor and Tsitsiklis (JMLR 5, 2004, pp. 623-648) prove T = Omega(H log(1/delta)) with H = sum_{i>=2} 1/Delta_i^2. Computed: 5 models with gaps 0.30/0.20/0.15/0.10 at delta = 0.05 needs at least 541 total pulls, 108 per model (H1 = 1625/9 exactly, SymPy-verified). Exact binomial: one attempt separates a 0.70 model from a 0.50 model with probability 3/5 = 0.600; three attempts give 1371/2000 = 0.6855; 32 attempts each are needed for 95%. At gap 0.10 it is 134; at gap 0.05, 540. Normal approximation agrees within 2 trials at every gap tested.

Coarse tiering is cheaper and nearly rescues him: the epsilon-best bound (n/epsilon^2) ln(1/delta) gives 48 pulls per model at epsilon = 0.25 and 133 at epsilon = 0.15 — crucially INDEPENDENT of roster size, so 1, 5, 70 or 700 models cost the same per model. The operating range is 10 to 300, not 2 to 3, and not 300 uniformly.
is_the_wheel_already_invented:
Yes, three times over, and one of the three is his exact design already built, measured and published.

1. THE RECURSION IS SEQUENTIAL HALVING. Karnin, Koren and Somekh, "Almost Optimal Exploration in Multi-Armed Bandits", ICML 2013 (PMLR 28:1238-1246), Algorithm 2. Introduced 2013, ported to hyperparameter selection by Jamieson and Talwalkar (AISTATS 2016, PMLR 51:240-248), parallelised as ASHA (Li et al., MLSys 2020, arXiv:1810.05934). His "assess the best, recurse on the rest" IS the halving skeleton.

2. THE DIFFICULTY LADDER IS COMPUTERIZED ADAPTIVE TESTING. "Hard item first, easier item if you fail, recurse" is the CAT item-selection rule, built on Item Response Theory. Lord's self-scoring flexilevel test (1971); Weiss's stratified-adaptive ("stradaptive") model (1973), which bins the item bank into 9 difficulty strata — his tiers; Birnbaum's 2PL model (1968) supplying the maximum-Fisher-information selection rule. Waters (1975) measured stradaptive testing at 19.2, 26.5 and 31.5 items per subject against 48.4 conventional — about a 2x saving, not 100x.

3. HIS COMPLETE SYSTEM IS ALREADY PUBLISHED. Balkır, Pernthaller, Basaldella, Hernández-Orallo and Collier, "Confident Rankings with Fewer Items: Adaptive LLM Evaluation with Continuous Scores", arXiv:2601.13885v2 (14 Sep 2026). It is IRT-based adaptive testing extended to continuous scores, with an uncertainty-aware multi-model ranker, pairwise-adjacent stopping at confidence 0.95, AND cost-aware allocation that "tests cheaper models to maximize uncertainty reduction per dollar spent" — his heterogeneity constraint, solved. Measured: Kendall tau 0.75 against ground-truth rankings using 2% of the full evaluation budget, 0.13 tau better than random sampling, 99% accuracy on confident predictions; adaptive stopping buys a further 32% item reduction and 39% cost saving over fixed-length CAT.

The number that matters most to him: that system uses 52 to 101 items per model, warms up with 5 items each, and REQUIRES a minimum of 10 per model before it will stop. Not 2 or 3.

Also already invented, for pieces he has not yet reached: racing (Maron and Moore, "Hoeffding Races", NeurIPS 1993 / NIPS 6, 1994; F-Race, Birattari, Stützle, Paquete and Varrentrapp, GECCO 2002; irace, López-Ibáñez et al., Operations Research Perspectives 3, 2016); cost-weighted multi-fidelity screening (Kandasamy et al., "The Multi-fidelity Multi-armed Bandit", NeurIPS 2016); and single-round distributed exploration with a sqrt(k) speedup (Hillel, Karnin, Koren, Lempel and Somekh, NeurIPS 2013).
strongest_disagreement:
Four contradictions, in descending severity.

1. "2 OR 3 SHOULD DO" IS REFUTED BY EXACT ARITHMETIC, AND AT HIS OWN ROSTER SCALES IT IS NOT EVEN EXECUTABLE. Exact binomial (SymPy, rationals): one attempt orders a 0.70-success model above a 0.50-success model with probability 3/5 = 0.600, barely above a coin flip; three attempts give 1371/2000 = 0.6855. For 95% correct ordering of that single pair: 32 attempts each. At gap 0.10, 134. At gap 0.05, 540. Scipy's binomial and the normal approximation z^2(p_a(1-p_a)+p_b(1-p_b))/(p_a-p_b)^2 agree within 2 trials at every gap tested (0.80, 0.30, 0.20, 0.10, 0.05). Worse, the mechanism he proposes cannot run at 3 attempts per model: Sequential Halving's round-0 allocation is t_0 = T/(n ceil(log2 n)), so with T = 3n the first round gets 0.429 pulls per arm at n = 70 and 0.300 at n = 700 — below one. His own constraint that the design must cope with 70 or 700 models mathematically forbids his own budget. He IS right that 300 uniformly is wasteful: at gaps of 0.30 to 0.50, 14 to 32 attempts suffice, and coarse tiering at epsilon = 0.25 needs 48 per model regardless of roster size. The honest range is 10 to 300, instrument-dependent.

2. GIVING LOSERS AN EASIER PROBLEM BREAKS THE MEASUREMENT SCALE. Sequential Halving holds the instrument fixed and varies budget precisely so scores stay comparable across rounds. He varies the instrument. Two models eliminated in different rounds have been measured on different, unequated tests, so no total order over the roster is defined. Psychometrics solves this with IRT's latent scale, which requires calibrated item parameters. His problems are randomly generated, hence uncalibrated — and calibration is not cheap: Balkır et al. used 17 models at 4 temperatures (68 configurations) to fit item parameters, and report that this one-time cost "breaks even after roughly 70 model evaluations on a dataset". They also had to FILTER items whose scores anti-correlate with ability; ATLAS (arXiv:2511.04689) measured 3% to 6% of items as having negative discrimination. A randomly generated hard problem can be one of those, in which case his top tier is populated by his worst models.

3. ONE PROBLEM IS THE WRONG UNIT, EVEN AT HIGH CONFIDENCE. Miller, "Adding Error Bars to Evals" (arXiv:2411.00640, Anthropic, Nov 2024) gives n = (z_{alpha/2}+z_beta)^2 (omega^2 + sigma_A^2/K_A + sigma_B^2/K_B)/delta^2 and concludes new evals need at least about 1,000 questions; his worked example reaches n = 969 for a 3% effect at 80% power. Resampling the SAME question K times only shrinks the within-question term: K = 2 cuts variance by 1/3, K = 4 by 1/2, with a floor at 2/3. One randomly generated problem leaves the between-question variance entirely unestimated, so there is no error bar on the tier assignment at all.

4. HIS KNOCKOUT BRACKET IS PROVABLY THE WORST MEMBER OF ITS OWN FAMILY, AND THE OBVIOUS PATCH DOES NOT WORK. Beygelzimer, Langford and Ravikumar, "Error-Correcting Tournaments" (ALT 2009), Corollary 1: single-elimination has regret ratio at most ceil(log2 n) — one upset permanently removes the best player. Their Section on failed strategies states that making every match redundant 2k-1 times yields "a regret ratio of at least log2 n, no better than the non-redundant single-elimination tournament", and that eliminating after k losses with arbitrary pairing also fails, an argument they note "applies to a Swiss tournament". Their k-elimination fix needs nk comparisons at O(k + log n) depth; k = 4 ln n buys regret ratio 5.5 at depth 22 ln n. Separately, dueling-bandit treatment (Gharat, Karamchandani and Nair, arXiv:2609.30360, 24 Sep 2026) requires a Condorcet winner to exist. If model strength is intransitive across task classes, the bracket has no well-defined answer at all.
open_problems: No published method combines fixed-confidence best-arm identification WITH per-arm degradation detection AND re-admission of previously eliminated arms. Change-detection bandits (CUSUM-UCB, Liu, Lee and Shroff, arXiv:1711.03539, local per-arm restarts; M-UCB, Cao, Wen, Kveton and Xie, AISTATS 2019, global restarts, regret O(sqrt(MKT log T)); GLR-klUCB, Besson and Kaufmann, JMLR 23, arXiv:1902.01575) all target cumulative regret, not identification. ASHA's rolling base-rung admission is the closest existing mechanism for honouring 'no model is ever permanently set aside', but it has no identification guarantee attached.

COMMON-MODE DEGRADATION BREAKS THE STANDARD STOPPING RULE. Zierahn, Koolen, Agrawal, Katsimerou and van der Hoeven, 'Best Arm Identification for Bandits with Shifting Means' (arXiv:2610.10488v1, 07 Oct 2026), Lemma 9: under an unobserved common shift the generalised-likelihood-ratio test statistic 'is uniformly 0 at all times, irrespective of the observed data'. A GLRT that models the shift never stops; one that ignores it is not delta-correct. Track-and-Stop inherits the failure. Their ISM fix costs 4(sigma^2+U^2) sum 1/Delta^2 ln(1/delta), so a shift bound U equal to sigma doubles the sample complexity and U = 3 sigma multiplies it by 10. This matters concretely here: if several seats share one account or one provider, throttling is a common-mode shift, and per-arm detectors will misread it as arm-specific decay.

FULLY DECENTRALISED BEST-ARM IDENTIFICATION WITH NO COORDINATOR IS NOT SOLVED. Hillel, Karnin, Koren, Lempel and Somekh (NeurIPS 2013) show one round of communication buys a sqrt(k) speedup and prove that is essentially optimal for that regime, with the full factor-k speedup needing communication logarithmic in 1/epsilon. Szorenyi, Busa-Fekete, Hegedus, Ormandi, Jelasity and Kegl, 'Gossip-based distributed stochastic bandit algorithms' (ICML 2013, PMLR 28), adapt bandits to peer-to-peer networks but target regret. More seriously: all of this literature assumes an HONEST scorer. In a BitTorrent-style topology a peer reports its own result, and no bandit paper found addresses a participant that misreports its score. That is a mechanism-design and Byzantine-agreement problem, not a bandit problem.

THE FIXED-BUDGET UPPER BOUND DOES NOT MEET THE LOWER BOUND. Karnin et al. state plainly that because H/H2 lies between 1 and ln(2n), 'our upper bound in the fixed budget setting is not directly comparable to the above lower bound'. Audibert, Bubeck and Munos (COLT 2010) prove no forecaster can achieve exp(-cn/H2) for all distributions, so H1 is the true hardness while H2 drives the bounds. Practically: for 6 models with one close rival at gap 0.05, the Sequential Halving budget formula T = 8 H2 ceil(log2 n) ln(3 ceil(log2 n)/delta) demands 99,705 pulls where the Mannor-Tsitsiklis floor is 1,271. Two orders of magnitude of slack sit between theory and the floor. Track-and-Stop (Garivier and Kaufmann, COLT 2016, PMLR 49:998-1027) closes it asymptotically as delta tends to 0, but the guarantee is asymptotic and the allocation is non-unique when several arms tie for best.

CROSS-TASK TRANSFER IS UNJUSTIFIED. Ranking on one mathematics problem and then routing all work by that ranking assumes capability is a scalar that transfers. Contextual bandits are the correct frame (Li, Chu, Langford and Schapire, WWW 2010, pp. 661-670), and OrcaRouter (arXiv:2605.30736) implements exactly that for model routing with a LinUCB contextual bandit — but it solves cold start by warming up OFFLINE on prompts whose reward is known for every arm, which is precisely the cold-start cost his scheme is trying to avoid. Sample complexity in the contextual setting scales with the number of task classes, so a per-task-class ranking multiplies the budgets above by the number of classes.

NO BOUND EXISTS FOR A COMPOSITE SCORE. His 'top' is a bundle: solved fastest, used tools, wrote proofs and falsifiers, cheapest. Every bound cited here assumes a scalar reward. Multi-objective fixed-confidence identification exists (arXiv:2501.13607) but returns a Pareto set, not a tier order, and the bundle's components have radically different variances: a continuous cost measure with coefficient of variation 0.3 and a 50% relative gap needs 6 samples, while a binary pass/fail at gap 0.10 needs 134. Collapsing them into one score before measuring destroys that distinction and silently inherits the worst component's sample complexity.

ITEM-BANK EXHAUSTION UNDER IMPROVING MODELS. GETA (arXiv:2406.14230) notes that conventional adaptive testing 'impractically assumes the difficulty completeness of the pool', which causes overestimation as models improve. His random generation is a partial answer, but a randomly generated problem has unknown difficulty, so the ladder cannot be positioned until after the fact. On-the-fly item generation WITH simultaneous difficulty calibration is an open problem.

mechanisms.name: Sequential Halving (fixed budget)
mechanisms.what_it_does: Splits a total budget T evenly across ceil(log2 n) rounds. In round r each surviving arm gets t_r = floor(T / (|S_r| ceil(log2 n))) pulls; the empirically worse half is dropped. One arm remains. Error at most 3 log2(n) exp(-T / (8 H2 log2 n)), with H2 = max_{i != 1} i/Delta_i^2 (Theorem 4.1). Equivalently T = O(H2 log n log(log n / delta)).
mechanisms.citation: Zohar Karnin, Tomer Koren, Oren Somekh, "Almost Optimal Exploration in Multi-Armed Bandits", ICML 2013, PMLR 28:1238-1246, https://proceedings.mlr.press/v28/karnin13.pdf (Algorithm 2, Theorem 4.1)
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: Assumes nothing. No prior, no model names, no capability estimate. Round 0 samples every arm uniformly, which is exactly his 'assume no capability at the outset'. It also needs no knowledge of the gaps or of H1, unlike UCB-E.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: It does not. Pulls are counted, not priced, so a desktop and a supercomputer are charged identically. Cost-awareness must be bolted on (see MF-UCB and the cost-aware entries).
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: Transfers directly and should be adopted as the skeleton. What breaks: (a) elimination is permanent, violating 'no model is ever permanently set aside' — needs an ASHA-style rolling re-admission; (b) it is synchronous, so a slow seat stalls a whole rung, contradicting the no-central-server goal; (c) the budget is unforgiving at his roster scales — with T = 3n, round 0 gets 0.429 pulls per arm at n = 70 and 0.300 at n = 700, i.e. the algorithm cannot execute. Measured budgets from Theorem 4.1 at delta = 0.05: 24,926 pulls for 5 models with gaps 0.30/0.20/0.15/0.10; 308,956 for 70 models with gaps spanning 0.05 to 0.60; 7,273,855 for 700 models with gaps from 0.02.

mechanisms.name: Exponential-Gap Elimination (fixed confidence)
mechanisms.what_it_does: The fixed-confidence twin of halving. In round r it targets arms with Delta_i > 2^-r, sampling each surviving arm t_r = (2/eps_r^2) ln(2/delta_r) times with eps_r = 2^-r/4 and delta_r = delta/(50 r^3), and uses Median Elimination to estimate the best mean. Theorem 3.1: identifies the optimal arm with probability at least 1-delta using O(sum_{i>=2} Delta_i^-2 log((1/delta) log(1/Delta_i))) pulls.
mechanisms.citation: Karnin, Koren and Somekh, ICML 2013, Algorithm 1 and Theorem 3.1; Median Elimination from Even-Dar, Mannor and Mansour, "Action Elimination and Stopping Conditions for the Multi-Armed Bandit and Reinforcement Learning Problems", JMLR 7 (2006) 1079-1105, https://jmlr.csail.mit.edu/papers/volume7/evendar06a/evendar06a.pdf
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: No prior needed; the per-round accuracy eps_r is scheduled rather than estimated, so it works from zero knowledge. Only delta is supplied by the user.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Not at all, same as Sequential Halving.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: This is the better fit for CDSFL than the fixed-budget form, because the founder cares about CORRECTNESS of tier assignment rather than exhausting a fixed spend. It is within a doubly-logarithmic factor of optimal. What breaks: Median Elimination's hidden constants are known to be large (noted in Hassidim, Kuperstein and Sharma, "An Optimal Elimination Algorithm for Learning a Best Arm", NeurIPS 2020, arXiv:2006.11647), so the asymptotic bound understates small-roster cost. For 5 or 6 seats, measure empirically rather than trusting the O-notation.

mechanisms.name: Mannor-Tsitsiklis sample-complexity lower bound
mechanisms.what_it_does: Proves that for a wide variety of reward setups, ANY policy needs T = Omega(H log(1/delta)) pulls where H = sum_{i>=2} 1/Delta_i^2. For the easier epsilon-best-arm problem the bound is Omega((n/eps^2) log(1/delta)), matched by Median Elimination. This is the floor nothing can get under.
mechanisms.citation: Shie Mannor and John N. Tsitsiklis, "The Sample Complexity of Exploration in the Multi-Armed Bandit Problem", JMLR 5 (2004) 623-648, https://www.jmlr.org/papers/volume5/mannor04b/mannor04b.pdf. Cite the JMLR version: the paper itself states that a lower bound in the preliminary 2003 version was valid only under an additional restriction on policies.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: It is the cold-start budget. It tells you the minimum measurement you must buy before any ranking claim is admissible, with no assumptions about which arm is best.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Counts pulls, not money. Under heterogeneous costs the binding bound is the cost-aware one (see Kanarios et al. and DCTAS).
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: Transfers as the arbiter of the 300-versus-3 dispute, and it settles it against him. Computed at delta = 0.05 (SymPy exact rationals and NumPy agree): 5 models with gaps 0.30/0.20/0.15/0.10 give H1 = 1625/9 = 180.556 and T >= 541, i.e. 108 per model; 5 models with gaps 0.10/0.08/0.06/0.05 give T >= 2,798, i.e. 560 per model; 6 models with one rival at gap 0.05 give T >= 1,271. Easy rosters are cheap: gaps of 0.50/0.40/0.30/0.20 need only T >= 139, i.e. 28 per model. The epsilon-best form is the one he actually needs for TIERS, and it is per-model constant in roster size: 48 pulls per model at eps = 0.25, 133 at eps = 0.15, 300 at eps = 0.10, 1,198 at eps = 0.05 — identical for n = 5, 70 and 700. That constant-per-model property is exactly the 'cope with 1, 5, 70 or 700 without redesign' property he asked for, and it is already a theorem.

mechanisms.name: Successive Rejects and UCB-E
mechanisms.what_it_does: Successive Rejects runs n-1 phases, dropping the empirically worst surviving arm each phase on a precomputed schedule; error is exponential in n/(log(2K) H2). UCB-E is a high-exploration UCB index that finds the best arm in about H rounds but requires knowing H. The paper defines H1 = sum_i 1/Delta_i^2 and H2 = max_i i/Delta_(i)^2, proves H2 <= H1 <= log(2K) H2, and proves no forecaster can achieve exp(-cn/H2) for all distributions.
mechanisms.citation: Jean-Yves Audibert, Sebastien Bubeck, Remi Munos, "Best Arm Identification in Multi-Armed Bandits", COLT 2010, http://sbubeck.com/COLT10_ABM.pdf
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: Successive Rejects needs no knowledge of H1 and no prior, so it is cold-start clean. UCB-E is NOT: it needs the exploration parameter tuned to problem hardness, which is unknown at the outset. The paper's adaptive-UCB-E variant estimates H online but has no theoretical guarantee.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: No cost model.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: Successive Rejects transfers and is a drop-in alternative to Sequential Halving; it rejects one arm per phase rather than half, which is gentler on a small roster of 5 or 6 seats where halving overshoots. Do NOT adopt UCB-E: requiring H in advance is equivalent to requiring the gap structure, which is the thing being measured, and the only variant that avoids that has no guarantee. The H1-versus-H2 result is the warning that fixed-budget guarantees are stated in the wrong hardness measure.

mechanisms.name: Computerized Adaptive Testing with Item Response Theory
mechanisms.what_it_does: Estimates a latent ability parameter theta by choosing each next item to maximise Fisher information at the current theta estimate; a failed item is followed by an easier one, a passed item by a harder one. Item difficulty and discrimination are calibrated in advance, which puts items and abilities on ONE common scale so scores from different item sequences remain comparable.
mechanisms.citation: F. M. Lord, "The self-scoring flexilevel test", Journal of Educational Measurement, 1971; D. J. Weiss, "The Stratified Adaptive Computerized Ability Test", Research Report 73-3, University of Minnesota, 1973; A. Birnbaum, two-parameter logistic model, in Lord and Novick, Statistical Theories of Mental Test Scores, 1968; C. W. Waters, empirical stradaptive study, 1975 (ERIC ED118604)
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: Starts every examinee at the item-bank median difficulty with a diffuse prior on ability, then converges. This is precisely his 'assume no capability at the outset', solved in 1973. BUT it requires a CALIBRATED item bank, which is the real cold-start cost and the part his randomly generated problems do not supply.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Ability is measured on one latent scale regardless of examinee, so a weak and a strong examinee are comparable despite answering disjoint item sets. That is the direct answer to 'it doesn't make sense to pitch a little desktop PC against an entire supercomputer': you do not have to pit them against each other at all, because both are located on the same theta scale.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: This is the missing half of his design and should be adopted. His difficulty ladder IS the CAT item-selection rule; without IRT's equating he has a ladder with no common scale, so scores from round 1 and round 2 cannot be combined into one ranking. What breaks if adopted: the item bank must be calibrated, and randomly generated problems have unknown difficulty AND unknown discrimination. Measured honestly, the saving is modest: Waters (1975) reports 19.2, 26.5 and 31.5 items per subject for three stradaptive strategies against 48.4 conventional — roughly 2x, not the 100x his 2-or-3 figure implies.

mechanisms.name: Continuous-score adaptive multi-model ranker with cost-aware allocation
mechanisms.what_it_does: Extends IRT-based adaptive testing from binary to continuous bounded scores by replacing the Bernoulli response with a heteroskedastic normal. Adds an uncertainty-aware ranker that stops when every ADJACENT model pair is separated at confidence gamma = 0.95 or the budget is exhausted, and a cost-aware allocation rule that, when a pair needs more evidence, preferentially tests the cheaper model to maximise uncertainty reduction per unit spend. Items with negative score-ability correlation are filtered out of the pool.
mechanisms.citation: Esma Balkir, Alice Pernthaller, Marco Basaldella, Jose Hernandez-Orallo, Nigel Collier, "Confident Rankings with Fewer Items: Adaptive LLM Evaluation with Continuous Scores", arXiv:2601.13885v2 [cs.CL], 14 Sep 2026, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2601.13885 (Algorithm 1)
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: Initialises theta ~ N(median of item difficulties, 25), then administers n_init warm-up items per model by maximum-Fisher-information selection. The expensive part is a one-time item calibration: they used 17 models at 4 temperature settings, 68 configurations, and report it 'breaks even after roughly 70 model evaluations on a dataset'.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Explicitly. Each model carries a per-item cost c_m; allocation divides expected information by cost, and the total budget B is a cost budget distributed flexibly across models rather than a fixed item count per model. Adaptive stopping yields 32% fewer items and 39% lower cost than fixed-length CAT.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: This is his design, built. Adopt it rather than re-deriving it. Headline measurements: Kendall tau 0.75 against ground-truth rankings at 2% of the full evaluation budget, 0.13 tau above random sampling, 99% accuracy on confident predictions; validated on 5 benchmarks across n-gram, embedding and judge-based metrics with 21 models from 6 families. The number that refutes his budget estimate: 52 to 101 items per model administered, 5 warm-up items, and a hard MINIMUM of 10 items per model before stopping is permitted. What breaks if adopted: it needs calibration data from models held out of the ranking, so a roster of 1 cannot be ranked at all, and a roster of 5 or 6 must borrow calibration from elsewhere.

mechanisms.name: Hyperband (the n versus B/n hedge)
mechanisms.what_it_does: Solves the problem that Successive Halving forces an arbitrary choice between many candidates with small budgets each and few candidates with large budgets each. Hyperband grid-searches over feasible values of n for fixed B, running one Successive Halving bracket per value; each bracket costs about B, and a full execution costs (s_max + 1) B. Larger n means smaller starting resource r and more aggressive early stopping.
mechanisms.citation: Lisha Li, Kevin Jamieson, Giulia DeSalvo, Afshin Rostamizadeh, Ameet Talwalkar, "Hyperband: A Novel Bandit-Based Approach to Hyperparameter Optimization", JMLR 18 (2018) 1-52, https://www.jmlr.org/papers/volume18/16-558/16-558.pdf
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: No prior required. It hedges the one free parameter halving cannot set from zero knowledge, which is how aggressively to prune on the first look.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Resource is one scalar dimension (iterations, data, time), so heterogeneous participants are not distinguished.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: Relevant precisely because the founder's scheme hard-codes the most aggressive bracket: 1 attempt per model, prune immediately. Hyperband exists because that choice is known to be unsafe when the cheap signal is a poor proxy for the expensive one. Adopt the bracket hedge rather than committing to a single aggressiveness. What breaks: the (s_max + 1) B multiplier means Hyperband is strictly more expensive than one halving run, which cuts against his 'absurdly too many attempts' instinct; the trade is robustness bought with spend.

mechanisms.name: ASHA (asynchronous successive halving)
mechanisms.what_it_does: Removes the synchronisation barrier from Successive Halving. Configurations are promoted to the next rung whenever a promotion is available rather than waiting for a rung to complete; when no promotion is available, a new configuration is added to the base rung. The number of configurations need not be specified in advance.
mechanisms.citation: Liam Li, Kevin Jamieson, Afshin Rostamizadeh, Ekaterina Gonina, Moritz Hardt, Benjamin Recht, Ameet Talwalkar, "A System for Massively Parallel Hyperparameter Tuning", MLSys 2020, arXiv:1810.05934, https://arxiv.org/pdf/1810.05934
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: Same as halving: uniform at the base rung, no prior. Additionally it does not require pre-specifying how many candidates to evaluate, so a roster that grows mid-run is handled natively.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Indirectly but importantly. The paper states synchronous halving 'is susceptible to stragglers' and reports simulated experiments showing ASHA more robust than synchronous halving to stragglers AND dropped jobs. A desktop among supercomputers IS a straggler; a dropped job IS a flaky endpoint.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: The single most directly useful engineering result for his constraints. It answers three at once: no synchronisation barrier (his no-central-server requirement), tolerance of slow and failing participants (his heterogeneity requirement), and a continuously refilled base rung (his 'no model is ever permanently set aside' requirement — a demoted model re-enters at the bottom instead of being deleted). What breaks: promotion decisions are still made against a shared rung state, so it is asynchronous but not coordinator-free. Going fully peer-to-peer needs the gossip or one-shot-communication results, and those carry no identification guarantee.

mechanisms.name: Hoeffding Races, F-Race and irace
mechanisms.what_it_does: Evaluate all candidates on a common stream of problem instances, and after each instance drop every candidate that is statistically dominated, so the remaining compute concentrates on the survivors. Hoeffding Races uses Hoeffding's bound and is distribution-free. F-Race substitutes Friedman's non-parametric two-way analysis of variance by ranks, which uses only the RANKING of candidates on each instance. irace wraps racing in an iterated loop that resamples the candidate population between races, and offers Friedman plus paired t-tests with Bonferroni or Holm correction.
mechanisms.citation: Oded Maron and Andrew W. Moore, "Hoeffding Races: Accelerating Model Selection Search for Classification and Function Approximation", NeurIPS 1993 / Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 6, 1994; Mauro Birattari, Thomas Stutzle, Luis Paquete, Klaus Varrentrapp, "A Racing Algorithm for Configuring Metaheuristics", GECCO 2002; Manuel Lopez-Ibanez, Jeremie Dubois-Lacoste, Leslie Perez Caceres, Mauro Birattari, Thomas Stutzle, "The irace package: Iterated racing for automatic algorithm configuration", Operations Research Perspectives 3 (2016) 43-58, https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2214716015300270
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: Fully uninformed start: every candidate begins with equal standing and elimination is driven entirely by observed instance-level results. irace adds a resampling step so new candidates enter later races, which is a re-admission mechanism.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: F-Race's rank-based test is the key asset. Because Friedman uses only within-instance RANKINGS, it is invariant to per-instance scale, so a problem that is uniformly hard for everyone does not distort the comparison. It does not price compute, however.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: Transfers immediately and is more robust than the mean-based halving tests for CDSFL's setting, because seat scores on a single hard problem are heavy-tailed and a rank test does not care. irace is mature, documented, and installable, so there is nothing to build. What breaks: Hoeffding Races is described in the follow-on literature as relatively conservative (it imposes no distributional assumptions and therefore eliminates slowly), so it will spend more than halving on an easy roster; and racing in its classic form is a fixed-sample test applied sequentially, which is not anytime-valid — a sequential test or confidence sequence is needed if the stopping decision is re-examined after every instance.

mechanisms.name: Track-and-Stop and the instance-optimal fixed-confidence complexity
mechanisms.what_it_does: Characterises the exact complexity of fixed-confidence best-arm identification. The lower bound states that the expected stopping time divided by log(1/delta) has liminf at least T*(mu), with the per-instance form E[tau_delta / T*(mu)] >= kl(delta, 1-delta). Track-and-Stop tracks the optimal sampling proportions implied by that lower bound, plugging in current empirical means, and stops by a Chernoff-style test when Z(t) >= log(1/delta). It is asymptotically optimal.
mechanisms.citation: Aurelien Garivier and Emilie Kaufmann, "Optimal Best Arm Identification with Fixed Confidence", COLT 2016, PMLR 49:998-1027, https://arxiv.org/abs/1602.04589; see also Kaufmann, Cappe and Garivier, "On the Complexity of Best-Arm Identification in Multi-Armed Bandit Models", JMLR 17 (2016), http://www.jmlr.org/papers/volume17/kaufman16a/kaufman16a.pdf
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: Needs forced exploration to get started, because the optimal proportions depend on the unknown means and are estimated by plug-in. It is cold-start-capable but not cold-start-efficient: the early rounds are essentially uniform anyway.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: The base version prices nothing, but the framework extends: cost-aware variants optimise in a cost-normalised design space (see DCTAS).
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: Transfers as the correct statement of what optimal allocation looks like — concentrate sampling on the pairs that are hard to separate, in the proportions T*(mu) dictates, not uniformly and not on the arms that have already lost. That is the principled version of what the founder is reaching for. TWO THINGS BREAK. First, optimality is asymptotic as delta tends to 0, so at delta = 0.05 on a 5-seat roster there is no guarantee the tracking has paid for itself. Second and far more seriously for CDSFL, its GLRT stopping rule FAILS under a common unobserved shift: the test statistic is uniformly 0 at all times irrespective of the data (Zierahn et al. 2026, Lemma 9). Any shared-account throttling or provider-wide quality change is such a shift.

mechanisms.name: Cost-aware best-arm identification
mechanisms.what_it_does: Replaces 'fewest pulls' with 'least money'. Two distinct formulations exist and they are not interchangeable: (a) find the arm with the best REWARD-TO-COST RATIO at fixed confidence, which requires estimating rewards and costs jointly and therefore needs MORE sampling than the reward-only problem; (b) find the best-reward arm while minimising cumulative acquisition cost, by optimising the allocation in a cost-normalised design space. Both come with lower bounds that the proposed elimination or Track-and-Stop-style algorithms asymptotically match, and in both the sample complexity grows logarithmically in 1/delta and linearly in the number of arms.
mechanisms.citation: "Cost-aware Best Arm Identification in Stochastic Bandits", ACM, DOI 10.1145/3712290, https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3712290 (ratio objective, epsilon-RCB for the PAC setting, lower bound under Bernoulli rewards and costs); Kanarios, Zhang and Ying, "Cost Aware Best Arm Identification", arXiv:2402.16710 (cost-minimising objective)
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: Both costs and rewards start unknown and are estimated online. The ratio formulation is explicitly harder at cold start because two quantities must be learned simultaneously, which the paper states 'greatly increases uncertainty and calls for more sampling'.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: This is the literature that exists for his heterogeneity constraint. Prices are per-arm and arbitrary, so a desktop and a supercomputer are compared on value for money rather than raw throughput.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: Transfers, and it forces a decision the founder has not yet made explicit. His 'most cost-effectively' is the RATIO objective, not the cost-minimisation objective, and the two have different winners: a model that is second-best but a tenth of the price wins on ratio and loses on reward. He must commit to one before any measurement is interpretable. What breaks: the ratio objective costs strictly more samples than ranking on reward alone, which pushes further against his 2-or-3 budget.

mechanisms.name: Cost-aware best-LLM identification with dueling feedback (DCTAS)
mechanisms.what_it_does: Frames best-model selection as fixed-confidence dueling-bandit identification with heterogeneous per-query costs: each comparison costs the sum of the two models' query costs and returns a winner. Theorem 1 gives a closed-form lower bound: expected cost divided by log(1/(4 delta)) is at least sum over suboptimal arms m of 1/alpha_m, where alpha_m = max_n d(p_mn, max(0.5, p_mn))/(c_m + c_n) and d is Bernoulli KL. DCTAS combines cost-aware tracking of the optimal allocation, forced exploration of any pair sampled fewer than sqrt(t) times, and a GLR Chernoff stopping rule; Theorem 3 shows it matches the lower bound asymptotically.
mechanisms.citation: Sarvesh Gharat, Nikhil Karamchandani, Jayakrishnan Nair, "Cost-Aware Best-LLM Identification using Dueling Feedback", arXiv:2609.30360v1 [cs.LG], 24 Sep 2026, https://arxiv.org/html/2609.30360
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: Starts from no preference information; forced exploration of under-sampled pairs at a sqrt(t) rate guarantees every pair is eventually seen. No prior over models.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Costs enter the lower bound itself through the (c_m + c_n) denominator, so the optimal allocation naturally avoids expensive pairings. Measured on real preference data at delta = 10^-10 over 100 trials, DCTAS cost 2,823 +/- 89 on text-to-image, 21.5 +/- 0.9 on text-to-text, 77.0 +/- 4.3 on vision and 1,015 +/- 28 on search, which is 2.4% to 5.9% cheaper than cost-unaware Track-and-Stop. A confidence-interval stopping variant was cheaper still, at 12.8 on text-to-text.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: This is the pairwise analogue of his knockout bracket, done properly, with the optimal pairing schedule derived rather than drawn from a bag. Adopt this in preference to random pairing. THE HARD CONSTRAINT HE MUST CHECK: it assumes a Condorcet winner exists, 'an arm that beats every other arm with a probability greater than 0.5'. If seat strength is intransitive across task classes — plausible when specialists exist — there is no Condorcet winner and the objective is undefined, which is a failure mode his bracket shares but does not detect. Also note the cost spread across task types (21.5 against 2,823) is a factor of 131: budget is task-class-specific, so a single global 'attempts per model' number is the wrong parameter to argue about.

mechanisms.name: Multi-fidelity bandits (MF-UCB)
mechanisms.what_it_does: Arms can be sampled at several fidelities; cheap fidelities give biased estimates at low cost. MF-UCB provably uses the low fidelities to explore all arms and eliminate low-reward arms, reserving high-fidelity plays for arms whose reward is close to optimal. Regret is cost-weighted, and a lower bound shows MF-UCB is near-optimal. The continuous-domain sibling, MF-GP-UCB, does the same for simple regret under a capital budget.
mechanisms.citation: Kirthevasan Kandasamy, Gautam Dasarathy, Junier Oliva, Jeff Schneider, Barnabas Poczos, "The Multi-fidelity Multi-armed Bandit", NeurIPS 2016, arXiv:1610.09726, http://papers.neurips.cc/paper/6592-the-multi-fidelity-multi-armed-bandit.pdf; and "Multi-fidelity Gaussian Process Bandit Optimisation", JAIR 66, arXiv:1603.06288
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: Starts cheap by design: all arms are explored at the lowest fidelity first, which is the cheapest possible cold start. No prior needed beyond knowing the fidelity costs and bias bounds.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Fidelity IS a cost axis, so this is the formalism in which 'use the easy problem first, the hard one only near the top' is a theorem rather than an intuition.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: This is the correct formalisation of his difficulty ladder, and it RUNS THE LADDER THE OTHER WAY. MF-UCB screens with the CHEAP, EASY, low-fidelity instrument across everyone, then spends the expensive high-fidelity evaluations only on the arms near the top where the decision is actually close. His scheme does the reverse: the expensive hard problem goes to everyone first, and the cheap easy problem goes to the losers whose exact ordering matters least. The proven version inverts his ordering. A documented failure mode supports the inversion: in the GP experiments a naive strategy that jumped straight to the top fidelity 'often stalled', becoming trapped near the optimum of the cheap approximation. What breaks: MF-UCB needs a bound on the bias between fidelities, i.e. a known relationship between easy-problem and hard-problem performance. Randomly generated problems of unverified difficulty supply no such bound.

mechanisms.name: Bandits with Knapsacks
mechanisms.what_it_does: Adds hard resource limits to bandits, so the learner solves a stochastic multi-dimensional knapsack problem alongside the exploration problem. Regret is measured against the best policy knowing the latent distribution, which may significantly outperform the best fixed arm. Normalised regret tends to zero as budget and optimal payoff grow, at the information-theoretically optimal rate; for dynamic procurement the bound is of order T/B^(1/4). The regret's dependence on the SMALLEST budget constraint is proven inevitable in the worst case.
mechanisms.citation: Ashwinkumar Badanidiyuru, Robert Kleinberg, Aleksandrs Slivkins, "Bandits with Knapsacks", FOCS 2013 (54th IEEE Symposium on Foundations of Computer Science); journal version Journal of the ACM 65(3), 2018, https://arxiv.org/pdf/1305.2545
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: No prior on rewards or resource consumption; both are learned online while the budget drains, which is the realistic cold start when every probe costs money.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Multiple simultaneous resource dimensions — tokens, wall-clock, GPU-hours, currency — each with its own budget. This is the only entry here that handles several distinct scarce resources at once, which is literally what the founder asked about.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: Transfers as the right frame for his actual question ('CPU/GPU, memory and storage capacity and cost'), because those are several budgets, not one. The result he most needs to hear: the achievable regret is governed by the SMALLEST budget constraint, and that dependence is provably unavoidable. So whichever resource is tightest sets the quality ceiling for the whole allocation, and adding slack to the others buys nothing. What breaks: the framework targets cumulative reward under budgets, not identification of a ranking, so it governs the exploitation phase rather than the cold-start tiering phase. The two objectives need separate budgets.

mechanisms.name: Non-stationary bandits: discounted and sliding-window UCB, and the variation budget
mechanisms.what_it_does: Two complementary characterisations of how much a changing environment costs. For abruptly switching rewards, D-UCB and SW-UCB both match a proven lower bound up to a logarithmic factor, giving regret of order sqrt(T) when the number of changes is finite. For gradually drifting rewards, constraining total variation of the mean rewards to a budget V_T yields minimax regret of order V_T^(1/3) T^(2/3) up to a logarithmic factor, with a matching Omega(V^(1/3) T^(2/3)) lower bound.
mechanisms.citation: Aurelien Garivier and Eric Moulines, "On Upper-Confidence Bound Policies for Switching Bandit Problems", ALT 2011, LNCS 6925, pp. 174-188 (earlier preprint arXiv:0805.3415); Omar Besbes, Yonatan Gur, Assaf Zeevi, "Stochastic Multi-Armed-Bandit Problem with Non-stationary Rewards", NeurIPS 2014, arXiv:1405.3316
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: Forgetting mechanisms (a discount factor or a window) mean the algorithm is permanently in a partial cold start, which is the point: it never fully commits to a stale estimate.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: No cost model.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: Transfers as the quantitative answer to 'how often must I re-measure'. The sharp lesson is the rate change: a stationary roster admits logarithmic regret, whereas a drifting one is stuck at T^(2/3), and that is a LOWER bound, not an artefact of a weak algorithm. So a one-off cold-start ranking has a shelf life that shrinks with drift, and the founder cannot rank once and route forever. What breaks: these are regret results, so they tell him how to keep EXPLOITING well under drift, not how to re-certify a tier assignment at fixed confidence. The combination he needs does not exist in the literature.

mechanisms.name: Change-detection bandits (CUSUM-UCB, M-UCB, GLR-klUCB)
mechanisms.what_it_does: Monitors each arm for a distribution shift and restarts the index when one is detected. CUSUM-UCB uses a two-sided CUSUM detector with 3 tuned parameters and performs LOCAL restarts, resetting only the arm where the change was detected. M-UCB compares the means of the two halves of a sliding window against a threshold, has 2 tuned parameters, and performs GLOBAL restarts, resetting all arms. M-UCB's regret is O(sqrt(M K T log T)) for M stationary segments, near-optimal in T up to a logarithmic factor; both achieve O(sqrt(Upsilon_T A T ln T)) when the number of breakpoints is known. Guarantees are stated in terms of mean detection delay and expected number of false alarms.
mechanisms.citation: Fang Liu, Joohyun Lee, Ness Shroff, "A Change-Detection based Framework for Piecewise-stationary Multi-Armed Bandit Problem", arXiv:1711.03539; Yang Cao, Zheng Wen, Branislav Kveton, Yao Xie, "Nearly Optimal Adaptive Procedure with Change Detection for Piecewise-Stationary Bandit", AISTATS 2019, arXiv:1802.03692; Lilian Besson and Emilie Kaufmann, "Efficient Change-Point Detection for Tackling Piecewise-Stationary Bandits", JMLR 23 (2022), arXiv:1902.01575
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: A detected change triggers a deliberate RETURN to cold start for the affected arm, which is exactly the founder's 'reassigned, not deleted' requirement expressed as an algorithm: the arm's history is discarded, not the arm.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: No cost model; detection thresholds are per-arm but prices are not represented.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: This is the mechanism for 'detect a model getting WORSE' and it should be adopted with LOCAL restarts (CUSUM-UCB or GLR-klUCB's local mode), not global. The reason is specific to his architecture: a global restart throws away every arm's history whenever any one arm moves, so a single flaky endpoint repeatedly destroys the whole roster's measurement. What breaks: these detectors assume changes are ARM-SPECIFIC. If several seats share one account or one provider, degradation is correlated across arms, a local detector will fire on several arms at once, and the system will read a provider-wide event as simultaneous independent model decay. Test for common-mode shift separately before trusting any per-arm alarm.

mechanisms.name: Best-arm identification under shifting means (the negative result)
mechanisms.what_it_does: Studies fixed-confidence identification when a common unobserved shift B_t, possibly adversarial and history-dependent, is added to every arm each round; only the GAPS are constant. Lemma 9: a GLRT that models the shifts has a test statistic that 'is uniformly 0 at all times, irrespective of the observed data', so it never stops; one that ignores the shifts is not delta-correct because the shifts inflate variance. Track-and-Stop inherits the failure. The proposed fix, ISM, uses importance-weighted evidence with forced exploration and stops at threshold ln((K-1)/delta); its sample complexity is 4(sigma^2 + U^2)(Delta_b*^-2 + sum_{a != a*} Delta_a^-2) ln(1/delta), with a matching lower bound within a factor of about 2 pi^2, roughly 20.
mechanisms.citation: Lukas Zierahn, Wouter M. Koolen, Shubhada Agrawal, Christina Katsimerou, Dirk van der Hoeven, "Best Arm Identification for Bandits with Shifting Means", arXiv:2610.10488v1 [stat.ML], 07 Oct 2026, https://arxiv.org/html/2610.10488 (Lemma 9, Theorems 2, 4, 6, 8)
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: ISM uses plug-in gap estimates with forced exploration, so it starts uninformed; U, a bound on the shift magnitude, must be supplied.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Not priced, but the shift term U is precisely where shared-infrastructure effects live.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: This is the most important negative result for CDSFL specifically, and it should change the design before any cold-start code is written. If seats share an account, a provider, or a time-of-day load pattern, their scores move together, and the standard stopping rule the whole fixed-confidence literature relies on becomes vacuous — not merely weak, but identically zero. The cost of handling it is quantified: sample complexity carries (sigma^2 + U^2) rather than sigma^2, so a shift bound equal to the noise doubles the budget and a shift 3 times the noise multiplies it by 10. Concretely: a shared-subscription channel is not a nuisance to be averaged out, it is a term in the sample-complexity formula.

mechanisms.name: Error-correcting tournaments (the verdict on his knockout bracket)
mechanisms.what_it_does: Analyses pairwise tournaments against an adversary charged according to the skill difference of the pairs it missorts, with a per-round budget. Corollary 1: single elimination has regret ratio at most ceil(log2 n). The k-elimination family uses n k comparisons at O(k + log n) depth; k = 1 recovers single elimination with regret ratio log2 n, k = 4 ln n gives regret ratio 5.5 at depth 22 ln n, and k = c n gives 4 + 1/c at depth (4c+1) n. Lower bounds of 2 in general and 3 for near-oblivious depth are proved.
mechanisms.citation: Alina Beygelzimer, John Langford, Pradeep Ravikumar, "Error-Correcting Tournaments", ALT 2009, https://hunch.net/~jl/projects/reductions/mc_to_b/tournament.pdf (Corollary 1, Summary of Results, and the 'Simple Strategies that Do Not Work' section)
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: Assumes nothing about skills, which matches his 'names drawn from a bag'. Pairings are adaptive rather than random.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Skills are arbitrary reals in [0,1] and the adversary is charged by skill DIFFERENCE, so a mismatch between a weak and a strong participant is expensive for the adversary to exploit. There is no compute-cost model.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: His second mechanism is the k = 1 corner of this family, which is the worst member of it. Three findings matter. First, regret ratio log2 n means a single upset at any node permanently removes the best participant, and with 70 models that is about 7 chances to lose the winner. Second, THE OBVIOUS PATCH IS PROVED NOT TO WORK: repeating every match 2k-1 times on a balanced tree gives 'a regret ratio of at least log2 n, no better than the non-redundant single-elimination tournament'. Third, eliminating after k losses with arbitrary pairing also fails, and the authors note the argument 'applies to a Swiss tournament'. If he wants a bracket, it must be the k-elimination construction, not a knockout with replays. Marked not-applicable because his actual objective is a FULL RANKING with tiers, and a tournament returns one winner; pairwise identification with cost-aware allocation (DCTAS) or adjacent-pair stopping (Balkir et al.) is the right tool for a ranking.

mechanisms.name: PAC maximum selection by knockout with repeated comparisons
mechanisms.what_it_does: Shows that for the APPROXIMATE objective — return an element within epsilon of the maximum under noisy pairwise comparisons — a knockout structure with repeated comparisons per round is optimal up to a constant factor, against a lower bound of Omega((n/2) log(1/lambda)) comparisons.
mechanisms.citation: Moein Falahatgar, Alon Orlitsky, Venkatadheeraj Pichapati, Ananda Theertha Suresh, "Maximum Selection and Ranking under Noisy Comparisons", ICML 2017, arXiv:1705.05366, https://arxiv.org/pdf/1705.05366
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: No prior; comparison probabilities are estimated as the bracket proceeds, with the number of repeats per round set by the target accuracy.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Comparison-based, so absolute score scale is irrelevant — a point in its favour when participants differ wildly. No cost model.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: This is the honest counterweight to the previous entry, and the founder is entitled to it: a knockout is NOT universally bad. For the relaxed objective of returning a near-best participant, knockout with repeats is optimal up to a constant. The two results are compatible because they answer different questions — exact identification against an adversary versus epsilon-approximate selection under independent noise. What breaks for him: the optimality depends on REPEATED comparisons per round whose count is set by the accuracy target, which is the opposite of one match per pairing; and it returns a near-best single element, not a tiered ranking of the whole roster. His constraint that the whole roster be ranked rules this out as a complete answer.

mechanisms.name: Statistical power for evaluation-based ranking
mechanisms.what_it_does: Gives the exact number of eval items needed to distinguish two models. Required items n = (z_(alpha/2) + z_beta)^2 (omega^2 + sigma_A^2/K_A + sigma_B^2/K_B)/delta^2, where omega^2 = Var(x_A) + Var(x_B) - 2 Cov(x_A, x_B) and K is the number of resamples per item. Variance decomposes as Var(mu-hat) = (Var(x) + E[sigma^2])/n, so resampling the same item K times shrinks ONLY the within-item term: K = 2 cuts variance by 1/3, K = 4 by 1/2, K = 6 by 5/9, with a floor at 2/3. Paired analysis on per-question differences, not population summaries, is recommended; clustered standard errors can exceed naive ones by more than 3x (measured 1.34 against 0.44 on one eval, a ratio of 3.05).
mechanisms.citation: Evan Miller, "Adding Error Bars to Evals: A Statistical Approach to Language Model Evaluations", Anthropic, arXiv:2411.00640, November 2024, https://arxiv.org/html/2411.00640v1
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: It is the cold-start cost accounting: it tells you how much measurement a ranking claim requires before you have the ranking, with no prior.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Pairing exploits positive correlation between two models on the same items, so SE_paired = sqrt(SE_A^2 + SE_B^2 - 2 SE_A SE_B Corr). At correlation 0.5 this cuts variance by 1/3. Giving different models different items destroys that gain — which is exactly what his difficulty ladder does.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: Transfers and is the most actionable single item for him, because it converts 'how many attempts' into arithmetic. His worked example reaches n = 969 items for a 3% effect at 80% power, and the paper concludes new evals should have at least about 1,000 questions. Recomputed with his omega^2 = 1/9 and sigma^2 = 1/6: a 10% effect needs 349 items at K = 1 and 114 at K = 10; a 20% effect needs 88 at K = 1 and 29 at K = 10; a 30% effect needs 39 at K = 1 and 13 at K = 10. So 'about 300' is right for detecting a 10-percentage-point capability difference, and 'about 13' is right for a 30-point difference with 10 resamples. Neither is 2. TWO THINGS BREAK HIS DESIGN DIRECTLY. First, one randomly generated problem leaves Var(x), the between-item variance, entirely unestimated, so no error bar on the tier exists. Second, his ladder gives different models different items, which forfeits the paired-comparison variance reduction and the clustering adjustment at the same time.

mechanisms.name: Compressed benchmarks via item response theory
mechanisms.what_it_does: Fits an IRT model to a benchmark, evaluates a new model on a small curated subset, estimates its latent ability by maximum likelihood, and predicts performance on the remainder. A generalised estimator, gp-IRT, blends direct sampling with IRT prediction for robustness when probabilities are inaccurate. Reported: 100 curated examples suffice to estimate performance on a 14,000-example benchmark with average estimation error under 2%, reduction factors of 140x and 160x; robust to distribution shift including specialised models and models released after the IRT fit. A fully adaptive successor reduces required items by up to 90% while maintaining precision, matching whole-bank ability estimates with 41 items out of 5,600 at 0.157 mean absolute error, and measured 3% to 6% of items as having NEGATIVE discrimination.
mechanisms.citation: Felipe Maia Polo, Lucas Weber, Leshem Choshen, Yuekai Sun, Gongjun Xu, Mikhail Yurochkin, "tinyBenchmarks: evaluating LLMs with fewer examples", ICML 2024, PMLR 235, arXiv:2402.14992; ATLAS, "Adaptive Testing for LLM Evaluation: A Psychometric Alternative to Static Benchmarks", arXiv:2511.04689
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: A new model is placed on the existing latent scale from a small subset with no prior on that model, and the authors demonstrate robustness to models released after the IRT model was fitted. The calibration itself is the cold-start cost and is amortised across all later models.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Different models can be scored on different item subsets and still compared, because IRT places them on one latent scale. This is the mechanism that makes his 'different difficulty per tier' idea legitimate rather than incoherent.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: Transfers and is the cheapest route to his goal: calibrate once, then rank each new seat from roughly 41 to 100 items instead of thousands. It also supplies the number he is looking for, and it is about 100, not 2 or 3. THE SPECIFIC HAZARD HE MUST DESIGN AROUND: 3% to 6% of items were measured as NEGATIVELY DISCRIMINATING, meaning weaker models score higher on them. A single randomly generated problem has an unknown chance of being one of those, and if it is, his top tier is populated by his worst seats and nothing in his scheme detects it. Published systems filter such items using calibration data; random generation cannot.

mechanisms.name: Distributed and peer-to-peer exploration
mechanisms.what_it_does: Quantifies the communication cost of cooperative best-arm identification. With k players collaborating to find an epsilon-optimal arm, ONE round of communication suffices for a sqrt(k) speedup, and a lower bound shows this is in general the best possible for that regime; the full factor-k speedup is achievable with communication only logarithmic in 1/epsilon. The gossip line of work adapts stochastic bandit algorithms to peer-to-peer networks where each peer pulls one arm per iteration and then communicates with a few random peers.
mechanisms.citation: Eshcar Hillel, Zohar Karnin, Tomer Koren, Ronny Lempel, Oren Somekh, "Distributed Exploration in Multi-Armed Bandits", NeurIPS 2013, arXiv:1311.0800, https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2013/file/598b3e71ec378bd83e0a727608b5db01-Paper.pdf; Balazs Szorenyi, Robert Busa-Fekete, Istvan Hegedus, Robert Ormandi, Mark Jelasity, Balazs Kegl, "Gossip-based distributed stochastic bandit algorithms", ICML 2013, PMLR 28, https://proceedings.mlr.press/v28/szorenyi13.html
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: Uninformed start; the question addressed is how much coordination the cold start needs, not whether a prior is required.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Players are assumed homogeneous and honest, which is the gap.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: Transfers as the honest ceiling on his BitTorrent-style constraint, and the news is better than he might expect: a SINGLE round of communication already buys a sqrt(k) speedup, and that is provably the most one round can buy. So a near-coordinator-free design is not merely possible but has a known price. TWO THINGS BREAK. First, the gossip results target regret, not fixed-confidence identification, so there is no published identification guarantee over a gossip topology. Second and more fundamental: every result here assumes an HONEST scorer. In a peer-to-peer topology a participant reports its own result, and no paper found addresses a peer that misreports. That is Byzantine agreement and mechanism design, not bandit theory, and it is a genuine gap rather than a solved problem he can cite.

mechanisms.name: Contextual bandits with task class as context
mechanisms.what_it_does: Chooses an arm using features of the current query as well as of the arms, updating from the observed reward only for the chosen arm. The canonical linear-index algorithm is computationally efficient and motivated from learning theory. Applied to model routing, one production-oriented system uses a linear contextual bandit over lexical and sentence-embedding features with a configurable multi-model action space, and solves cold start by WARMING UP OFFLINE on a curated set of routing prompts for which every arm's reward is already known.
mechanisms.citation: Lihong Li, Wei Chu, John Langford, Robert E. Schapire, "A Contextual-Bandit Approach to Personalized News Article Recommendation", WWW 2010, pp. 661-670, DOI 10.1145/1772690.1772758; "OrcaRouter: A Production-Oriented LLM Router with Hybrid Offline-Online Learning", arXiv:2605.30736 (technical report, not peer-reviewed)
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: Badly, on its own: a contextual bandit must learn a reward model per context, so cold start is strictly harder than the context-free case. The production system's answer is to pay the cold-start cost OFFLINE against known rewards, which is the opposite of starting from zero.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Arm features can encode cost and capacity, so a desktop and a supercomputer are distinguishable as arms. Cost does not enter the objective unless explicitly added.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: Transfers as the refutation of a hidden assumption rather than as a mechanism to adopt. Ranking the roster on ONE mathematics problem and then routing ALL work by that order presumes capability is a transferable scalar. The contextual framing says reward depends on the context, so the correct object is a ranking PER TASK CLASS, and that multiplies every budget in this report by the number of classes. The production system's offline warm-up is the measured evidence that no one has made contextual cold start cheap. Deeper problem for CDSFL: contextual routing needs a reward signal per query, and the founder's reward is 'wrote a correct proof and a falsifier', which is expensive to grade — so the reward model is itself the bottleneck, not the allocation policy.

mechanisms.name: Fixed-budget best-arm identification applied to prompt and candidate selection
mechanisms.what_it_does: Treats a pool of candidates as the arms of a fixed-budget best-arm identification problem and allocates a limited evaluation budget among them using successive-halving-style identification rather than uniform evaluation. Reported improvements of 3% to 16% on average over baselines.
mechanisms.citation: Chengshuai Shi, Kun Yang, Zihan Chen, Jiaqi Li, Jing Yang, Cong Shen, "Efficient Prompt Optimization Through the Lens of Best Arm Identification" (TRIPLE), NeurIPS 2024, https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2024/file/b46bc1449205888e1883f692aff1a252-Paper-Conference.pdf
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: No prior over candidates; the budget is allocated adaptively from uniform first-round sampling.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Candidates are assumed equally priced; the budget is counted in evaluations.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: Transfers as the existence proof that the founder's framing — fixed evaluation budget, pool of candidates, identify the best — is already standard practice in adjacent work on candidate selection, with measured gains in the single-digit to mid-teens percent range over naive baselines. That magnitude is the honest expectation for adopting adaptive allocation: a real but modest improvement, not an order of magnitude. What breaks: it selects ONE best candidate for ONE task, whereas he needs a tiered ranking reused across tasks, which reintroduces the transfer problem.

mechanisms.name: Regret-minimising bandits (UCB1, Thompson sampling, epsilon-greedy)
mechanisms.what_it_does: Minimise CUMULATIVE reward loss rather than identify the best arm. UCB1 achieves logarithmic regret uniformly over time for all reward distributions with bounded support, needing no prior beyond knowing the support lies in [0,1]; the matching lower bound is Omega(log T). Thompson sampling, the oldest such heuristic, has a finite-time logarithmic bound and a problem-independent bound of O(sqrt(N T ln T)), with O(sqrt(N T ln N)) and a matching lower bound in the Gaussian case.
mechanisms.citation: Peter Auer, Nicolo Cesa-Bianchi, Paul Fischer, "Finite-time Analysis of the Multiarmed Bandit Problem", Machine Learning 47 (2002) 235-256, https://homes.di.unimi.it/~cesabian/Pubblicazioni/ml-02.pdf; T. L. Lai and Herbert Robbins, "Asymptotically efficient adaptive allocation rules", Advances in Applied Mathematics 6 (1985) 4-22; William R. Thompson (1933); Shipra Agrawal and Navin Goyal, "Further Optimal Regret Bounds for Thompson Sampling", AISTATS 2013, PMLR 31, and "Near-Optimal Regret Bounds for Thompson Sampling", Journal of the ACM 64(5), 2017
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: UCB1's exploration bonus is infinite for an unpulled arm, so every arm is tried once before any is repeated — a clean, parameter-free cold start. Thompson sampling starts from a prior, which conflicts with 'assume no capability' unless the prior is uniform.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Neither prices arms.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: Marked not-applicable deliberately, and this is the most common error in this space. Regret minimisation and best-arm identification are DIFFERENT objectives with different optimal strategies: a regret-minimising policy deliberately under-explores arms it believes are bad, because every exploratory pull costs reward, whereas identification requires sampling bad arms enough to CERTIFY they are bad. Using UCB1 or Thompson sampling to produce the founder's tier assignment will systematically under-measure the lower tiers and leave their ordering unresolved — which is precisely the part he wants, since he intends to reassign rather than discard them. These belong in the exploitation phase AFTER tiering, not in the cold start. The distinction is the reason the pure-exploration literature exists as a separate field (Bubeck, Munos and Stoltz, "Pure Exploration in Multi-Armed Bandits Problems", ALT 2009).
